extra.message: Missing authorization on delete-user API — Unauthenticated attacker can delete any user account in the system, including admins, causing account takeover/denial of service. [verified: token_required commented out (line 221-222); delete() performs unconditional DELETE FROM users by id with zero auth check.]

Hardcoded weak secret key and insecure session/debug config — Attacker who guesses/brute-forces the weak hardcoded secret can forge session cookies and JWTs to impersonate any user/admin; DEBUG=True can leak stack traces/source and enable the Werkzeug debugger RCE; HttpOnly=False exposes session cookies to XSS-based theft. [verified: SECRET_KEY is a hardcoded weak literal used for both Flask session signing and JWT signing/verification, and DEBUG=True plus HTTPONLY=False are both present with no override found.]

SQL Injection in dashboard search — Attacker can exfiltrate or manipulate arbitrary data from the SQLite database (other users' filenames, potentially UNION-based extraction of credentials) via the authenticated /dashboard?search= parameter. [verified: search_query is f-string interpolated directly into SQL at line 137 with no sanitization, unlike the parameterized query at line 140.]

Mass assignment / privilege escalation via /update_profile — Any authenticated low-privilege user can set their own role/permissions to admin, achieving full privilege escalation. [verified: role/permissions from request.form are accepted whenever present (lines 187-196) with no admin check, then written to the users table at line 234.]

Privilege escalation via mass assignment on profile update — A regular user can grant themselves admin role/permissions, escalating privileges. [verified: Duplicate of idx 3/6: no admin/ownership check gates role/permissions in update_profile before the DB write.]

Mass assignment / privilege escalation via role and permissions fields — Any authenticated user can self-promote to admin/elevated role or grant themselves arbitrary permissions stored in the DB, bypassing intended authorization tiers. [verified: Same as idx 3: role/permissions accepted from client form data with no authorization check before being written via the parameterized UPDATE at line 234.]

Broken access control / IDOR on profile API — Unauthenticated attacker can enumerate user_id values and dump PII (email, country, role, permissions, team) for every user in the system. [verified: token_required is commented out (line 152-153) and get() takes user_id from query args with no session/ownership check, returning full profile including role/permissions.]

Unauthenticated IDOR on profile API — Anonymous attacker can dump PII (email, country, role, permissions, team) for any user by iterating user_id values [verified: Same code path as idx 0: decorator commented out, user_id fully attacker-controlled, response includes PII and role/permissions.]

Privilege escalation chain via update-profile API sensitive fields — Combined with the mass-assignment bug in the web route, an attacker can permanently entrench admin role/permissions through the API as well. [verified: Line 201 gates sensitive_updates solely on current DB role of session['user_id'], and role can be set to admin via the web /update_profile mass-assignment path, after which this endpoint lets that same user freely modify role/permissions with no CSRF protection.]

SSRF via update_picture endpoint — Attacker can make the server issue requests to internal-only services (cloud metadata endpoint 169.254.169.254, internal admin panels, localhost services) and, since the response content-type/body is reflected back into a saved file and error messages are returned verbatim, can perform internal network reconnaissance and potentially retrieve internal service data. [verified: picture_url from JSON body is passed directly to requests.get() with no allow-list or internal-IP blocking, and no auth decorator guards the endpoint at all.]

Flask DEBUG mode enabled in production config — Attacker triggering any unhandled exception reaches the Werkzeug interactive debugger, exposing stack traces/source and potentially remote code execution via the debugger console [verified: DEBUG=True is set unconditionally in the shared Config class with no environment-based override, enabling the Werkzeug debugger in production deployments.]

Path traversal on file upload — Attacker can upload a file with a name like '../../../etc/cron.d/x' or overwrite arbitrary files within reach of the process, potentially achieving RCE or overwriting application files. [verified: file.filename used raw in os.path.join at line 262-263 with no secure_filename or traversal check before file.save.]

Path traversal in file delete — Deletion of arbitrary files reachable by the process's filesystem permissions (since upload also allows arbitrary filenames/paths), leading to data loss or DoS. [verified: file_path is built from the raw URL filename before the ownership check, and even the DB-matched filename is never sanitized; combined with unsanitized upload (finding 1) an attacker can insert traversal filenames leading to arbitrary delete.]

Session cookie HttpOnly flag disabled — Any XSS on the site (e.g. the |safe-rendered fields below) can be used to steal the session cookie directly via JS, enabling full session hijacking [verified: SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=False is explicitly set with no other flag overriding it, exposing the session cookie to JS access.]

Missing authentication on profile picture retrieval — Unauthenticated attacker can enumerate and view any user's profile picture without logging in. [verified: Confirmed duplicate of idx 5: route at line 307-309 lacks any session check present in sibling routes.]

Weak password hashing (unsalted MD5) — If the SQLite database is exfiltrated (e.g. via the SQL injection above), all user passwords can be recovered via rainbow tables/brute force since MD5 is fast and unsalted. [verified: custom_hash uses unsalted MD5 for both storage (line 93) and login comparison (line 50), confirmed weak crypto with no salt/iteration.]
